prompt: It can reasonably be inferred from the passage that the octopus's color change is

choices.text: learned only gradually over the whole course of the animal's adult life
choices.rationale: The change happens in under a second, not slowly over a lifetime.

choices.text: perceptible to the octopus itself but not to other animals
choices.rationale: The octopus is colorblind, so it cannot perceive its own colors.

choices.text: produced by muscles widening sacs of pigment beneath the skin
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage states muscles widen the sacs to reveal color.

choices.text: triggered by the temperature of the surrounding seawater
choices.rationale: Temperature is never mentioned as a cause.

explanation: The text directly ties color change to muscles pulling on pigment sacs.

stimulus.title: The Color of Thought
stimulus.text: An octopus has no bones and, oddly, almost no color of its own. Yet in less than a second it can flush deep red with alarm or fade to match the speckled gray of a stone. Beneath its skin lie millions of tiny sacs of pigment, each ringed by muscle. When the muscles pull, the sacs widen and color blooms; when they relax, the color vanishes. Stranger still, the octopus is colorblind, so it cannot see the very hues it produces. Some researchers suspect its skin itself senses light, letting the animal paint a disguise it can never admire.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that a 'clean line' on a finished map represents

choices.text: a once-open question that exploration eventually answered
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says every clean line 'was once a question,' settled by explorers.

choices.text: a deliberate decoration much like a painted sea monster
choices.rationale: Clean lines replaced decorations, not added them.

choices.text: a region that, even now, remains completely unknown
choices.rationale: Clean lines mark known, corrected regions.

choices.text: a mistake that no later mapmaker ever got around to correcting
choices.rationale: The line marks a settled answer, not an uncorrected mistake.

explanation: A clean line stands for a once-open question now resolved.

stimulus.title: The Edge of the Map
stimulus.text: Old maps are full of guesses. Where knowledge ran out, mapmakers filled the blank spaces with mountains they had never seen and coastlines that bent the wrong way. Some added sea monsters, less from belief than from a need to decorate the unknown. As explorers returned with measurements, the guesses were slowly corrected, and the monsters swam off the page. But a finished, accurate map can hide how hard it was to make. Every clean line was once a question, settled only by someone willing to sail past the edge of what was known and come back with an answer.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that the first version of the letter was

choices.text: the version he ultimately decided to send
choices.rationale: He sent none of the versions.

choices.text: written to confess how far from home he felt
choices.rationale: Confessing his homesickness describes the later realization, not the cheerful first draft.

choices.text: an honest account of his deep homesickness
choices.rationale: The honest account was the second version, not the first.

choices.text: more cheerful than Tomas actually felt
choices.rationale: Correct. He was cheerful 'as if homesickness were a thing he had outgrown,' though he had not.

explanation: The first draft put on cheerfulness he did not truly feel.

stimulus.title: The Unsent Letter
stimulus.text: Tomas wrote the letter three times before he stopped trying to send it. In the first version he was cheerful, listing the small triumphs of his new city as if homesickness were a thing he had outgrown. In the second he was honest, and the page filled with everything he missed until it embarrassed him. The third version said almost nothing at all. He kept that one folded in a drawer. Months later he found it again and realized the words he could not send had still done their work: writing them had let him admit, if only to himself, how far from home he truly felt.

prompt: The comparison to a fire extinguisher mainly suggests that the vault is

choices.text: dangerous and therefore risky to keep anywhere nearby
choices.rationale: No danger is implied.

choices.text: drawn upon constantly throughout every month of the year
choices.rationale: The passage hopes it is rarely needed.

choices.text: valuable precisely because it is ready even if it is rarely used
choices.rationale: Correct. Like an extinguisher, its worth lies in readiness for a rare emergency.

choices.text: useful for nothing other than literally putting out fires
choices.rationale: The analogy is about readiness, not literal firefighting.

explanation: The analogy stresses preparedness for an uncommon emergency.

stimulus.title: A Vault for Seeds
stimulus.text: Deep inside a frozen mountain, a vault holds something more valuable than gold: seeds. Hundreds of thousands of varieties of crops, gathered from around the world, rest in sealed packets at temperatures far below freezing. The cold slows the seeds' aging to a crawl, so that even after decades they can still sprout. The vault is a backup. If a war, flood, or disease wipes out a crop somewhere, a sample can be withdrawn and grown again. Its keepers hope it will rarely be needed, the way one hopes never to use a fire extinguisher. Its value lies precisely in being ready and almost never used.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that, before automation, a lighthouse's reliability depended on

choices.text: the sheer height of the tower above the surrounding water
choices.rationale: Height alone did not keep the light lit.

choices.text: the complete absence of storms along that stretch of coast
choices.rationale: Storms occurred and made the work dangerous.

choices.text: the constant nightly labor of a dedicated human keeper
choices.rationale: Correct. Keepers performed the nightly tasks that kept the light burning.

choices.text: electric lamps, timers, and remote sensors doing the work
choices.rationale: Timers and sensors came later, with automation.

explanation: Reliability rested on the keeper's constant labor.

stimulus.title: Keeping the Light
stimulus.text: For centuries, a lighthouse meant a keeper. Someone had to climb the tower each night, trim the wick, polish the lens, and wind the clockwork that turned the light. Storms made the work dangerous, and isolation made it lonely, but ships depended on that faithful beam. In the twentieth century, automation arrived. Electric lamps, timers, and remote sensors took over the tasks one by one, and keepers were gradually withdrawn. The lights still shine, more reliably than ever, yet something human slipped away with the last keeper. The machines kept the promise of the light; they could not keep its company.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that Nadia almost refused the loaner because she

choices.text: actually preferred instruments whose tuning pegs kept slipping
choices.rationale: She struggled with slipping pegs; she did not prefer them.

choices.text: felt unworthy of playing such a fine and valuable instrument
choices.rationale: Correct. 'It felt wrong to play something so fine' signals a sense of unworthiness.

choices.text: strongly disliked the pieces she was assigned for the recital
choices.rationale: Her feelings about the pieces are not the reason given.

choices.text: had never learned how to read the music set before her
choices.rationale: Nothing suggests she cannot read music.

explanation: Her hesitation stems from feeling the instrument was too fine for her.

stimulus.title: The Borrowed Violin
stimulus.text: Nadia had practiced on a school instrument so battered that two of its pegs slipped during every lesson. When her teacher handed her a loaner violin for the recital, she nearly refused; it felt wrong to play something so fine. But as she drew the bow across the strings, the tone opened like a window onto a bright street. Notes she had fought for all year now arrived easily, as if the instrument had been waiting for her. Afterward, returning it to its case, she understood that her old struggles had not been wasted. The fine violin had simply revealed the player she had quietly become.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that mixing glass colors during recycling

choices.text: has no real effect of any kind on the recycling process
choices.rationale: Mixing clearly has a negative effect.

choices.text: reduces the usefulness, and so the value, of the recycled material
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says mixing colors lowers the value of recycled glass.

choices.text: is actually required by most existing recycling regulations
choices.rationale: Sorting is recommended, not color mixing.

choices.text: improves the overall strength and clarity of the new bottles that result
choices.rationale: Mixing lowers value; it does not improve strength.

explanation: Mixed colors lower the recycled material's value, the passage states.

stimulus.title: The Endless Material
stimulus.text: Glass has a quiet superpower: it can be melted down and remade again and again without losing quality. A bottle recycled today can become a bottle next month, then another after that, in a loop that, in principle, never wears out. Compared with this ideal, reality lags. Much glass still ends up in landfills because collection is uneven and because mixing colors lowers the value of the recycled material. Sorting by color and keeping glass out of general trash would let more of it re-enter the loop. The material is willing; it is our systems, the author suggests, that need redesigning.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that draining and filling marshes most likely left coastal communities

choices.text: more exposed to the force of storms
choices.rationale: Correct. Since marshes blunt storms, removing them would increase exposure.

choices.text: better protected from rising seas
choices.rationale: Draining removed the buffer, reducing protection from the sea.

choices.text: wealthier from the carbon they stored
choices.rationale: Draining released, rather than profited from, stored carbon.

choices.text: surrounded by thicker marsh grasses
choices.rationale: Filling marshes destroys grasses rather than thickening them.

explanation: Removing the marsh buffer would leave communities more exposed to storms.

stimulus.title: The Quiet Buffer
stimulus.text: Where the land meets the sea, a salt marsh can look like wasteland: flat, muddy, and crossed by winding channels. Yet this drab landscape does remarkable work. Its dense grasses slow incoming waves, blunting the force of storms before they reach homes inland. The same grasses trap sediment, letting the marsh build itself upward as the sea slowly rises. Beneath the mud, roots store carbon that might otherwise warm the air. For years, marshes were drained and filled without much thought. Only later did people recognize that the unglamorous marsh had been protecting them all along, asking nothing in return.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that the delay between a bat's call and its echo tells the bat about an object's

choices.text: distance
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says the delay lets the bat judge how far away an object is.

choices.text: weight
choices.rationale: Weight is not part of what the echo reveals.

choices.text: color
choices.rationale: Color is never linked to the echoes.

choices.text: temperature
choices.rationale: Temperature is not mentioned.

explanation: The call-to-echo delay corresponds to distance.

stimulus.title: Seeing With Sound
stimulus.text: A bat hunting in pitch darkness does not bump into things. It calls out, often at pitches too high for humans to hear, and listens for the echoes that bounce back. From the delay between call and echo, the bat judges how far away an object is; from subtle shifts in the returning sound, it can tell whether the object is moving toward it or away. A moth's fluttering wing returns a different echo than a still leaf. So precise is this sense that some bats can snatch an insect from the air in total darkness. The world the bat perceives is built entirely of sound, a picture painted with echoes.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that the angle of the waggle run is meaningful because it

choices.text: relates the direction of the food to the position of the sun
choices.rationale: Correct. The angle against gravity encodes direction relative to the sun.

choices.text: reveals the particular color and scent of the flowers that were found
choices.rationale: Color is not encoded by the dance.

choices.text: indicates the current temperature inside the bees' hive
choices.rationale: Temperature is not mentioned.

choices.text: measures the age of the individual bee that is dancing
choices.rationale: The bee's age is irrelevant to the dance.

explanation: The angle's meaning comes from its relation to the sun's direction.

stimulus.title: Dances in the Dark
stimulus.text: A foraging honeybee that finds a rich patch of flowers cannot simply tell the hive where to go. Instead, it dances. On the vertical comb, in darkness, the bee runs a straight line while waggling its body, then loops back to repeat the move. The angle of that straight run, measured against the pull of gravity, encodes the direction of the flowers relative to the sun. The length of the run signals distance. Watching bees crowd around and follow, researchers realized they were seeing a kind of symbolic language, one that passes precise information without sight, sound, or a single spoken word.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that fog harvesting is most practical in places that have

choices.text: no moving air or wind of any kind at any time
choices.rationale: Steady winds are required, so 'no wind' is wrong.

choices.text: long, very cold winters lasting much of the year
choices.rationale: Cold winters are not mentioned as a requirement.

choices.text: heavy rainfall spread evenly throughout the whole year
choices.rationale: Such places would not need fog harvesting as much.

choices.text: frequent fog together with steady, reliable winds
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says it works only where fog is frequent and winds steady.

explanation: Suitability depends on frequent fog and steady wind.

stimulus.title: Catching Water From Air
stimulus.text: In a few dry coastal regions, drinking water can be harvested from fog. Tall mesh nets are strung across hillsides where moist air rolls in from the sea. As the fog drifts through, droplets cling to the mesh, merge, and trickle down into troughs and storage tanks. A single large net can collect many liters on a good day, enough to supplement a village's supply. The method is not a cure-all: it works only where fog is frequent and winds are steady, and the nets need upkeep. Yet in the right place, it turns a passing cloud into a dependable resource, using little more than gravity and patience.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that sea otters help kelp forests by

choices.text: anchoring the giant kelp firmly to the rocky seafloor
choices.rationale: The kelp anchors itself; otters do not anchor it.

choices.text: keeping the population of kelp-grazing urchins in check
choices.rationale: Correct. When otters vanish, urchins multiply and graze the kelp down, so otters limit urchins.

choices.text: providing the sunlight that the growing kelp needs
choices.rationale: Sunlight comes from the sun, not from otters.

choices.text: slowing the rapid growth of the kelp near the surface
choices.rationale: Otters do not slow kelp growth; their loss harms the kelp.

explanation: Otters help by controlling the urchins that would otherwise destroy the kelp.

stimulus.title: Forests Beneath the Waves
stimulus.text: Off some cool, rocky coasts grow forests that no hiker will ever walk through. Giant kelp, anchored to the seafloor, can stretch dozens of meters toward the surface, swaying in the current like trees in wind. These kelp forests shelter fish, snails, and otters, much as a woodland shelters birds and deer. The kelp grows astonishingly fast, sometimes half a meter in a single day, drinking sunlight near the surface. But the forest is fragile. Where otters vanish, sea urchins multiply and graze the kelp down to bare rock, leaving a barren the divers call an urchin desert. A single missing animal can unmake a whole forest.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that the coral record is valuable mainly because it

choices.text: can be created quickly in a laboratory whenever needed
choices.rationale: Coral grows over centuries; it is not made quickly in a lab.

choices.text: preserves data from times before people kept measurements
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage stresses conditions recorded 'before anyone thought to measure them.'

choices.text: remains perfectly readable without any special training
choices.rationale: The passage calls reading it a challenge requiring effort.

choices.text: shows exactly which species of fish lived nearby each year
choices.rationale: Nearby fish species are never mentioned.

explanation: Its value lies in capturing conditions from before instrument records existed.

stimulus.title: The Coral That Keeps Time
stimulus.text: A coral skeleton grows in fine bands, much like the rings of a tree. In bright, warm months the coral lays down thick layers; in cooler, dimmer months the layers thin. By slicing a coral and counting these bands, researchers can read a record of past seasons stretching back centuries. Even better, the chemistry trapped in each band hints at the water's temperature when it formed. So a single old coral can serve as a kind of diary, written not in words but in stone, recording conditions long before anyone thought to measure them. The challenge is learning to read a language no one designed to be read.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that seeds wear hooks in order to

choices.text: help the seeds spin like helicopters in the wind
choices.rationale: Spinning like a helicopter describes winged seeds, not hooked ones.

choices.text: make the seeds heavier so they fall straight down
choices.rationale: Hooks aid travel, not added weight to fall straight down.

choices.text: protect the seeds from being eaten by any animal
choices.rationale: Hooks help seeds catch a ride, not avoid being eaten.

choices.text: catch onto animals that carry them to new places
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says hooked seeds snag passing animals and hitch a ride.

explanation: Hooks let seeds catch onto animals for transport.

stimulus.title: Travelers Without Legs
stimulus.text: A plant cannot walk, yet its seeds must somehow leave the shadow of the parent and find open ground. Evolution has answered this need with a surprising range of tricks. Some seeds grow papery wings and spin away on the wind like tiny helicopters. Others wear hooks that snag the fur of passing animals, hitching a ride for miles. Still others hide inside sweet fruit, counting on an animal to eat them and carry them off, depositing them far away. Each method is a kind of bargain struck with the world around the plant. The seed that travels farthest is often the one with the best chance to grow where the parent's shade cannot reach.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that public voting was a problem chiefly because it

choices.rationale: Travel distance is never mentioned.

choices.text: let powerful people see and punish how others voted
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says open voting invited pressure and fear of retaliation.

choices.text: prevented neighbors from ever discussing politics
choices.rationale: Public voting did not stop political discussion.

choices.text: made the counting of votes slow and unreliable
choices.rationale: Vote-counting speed is not discussed.

explanation: The danger of public voting was exposure to pressure and punishment.

stimulus.title: The Secret Ballot
stimulus.text: It is easy to assume voting has always been private, but for a long time it was not. In many places people voted aloud or by a show of hands, in full view of employers, landlords, and neighbors. That openness invited pressure: a worker might think twice before voting against a boss who could see the choice. Reformers pushed for a printed ballot, marked alone and dropped in a box, so that no one need fear retaliation for an honest vote. The change seemed minor, a mere matter of paper, yet it shifted real power toward the ordinary voter, who could now decide without an audience.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that before locks existed, inland water travel was

choices.text: faster than any later canal-based travel
choices.rationale: No claim is made that earlier travel was faster.

choices.text: carried out mostly by very large ocean ships
choices.rationale: Ocean ships are never mentioned.

choices.text: limited by differences in a river's elevation
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says elevation 'blocked boats from traveling far inland.'

choices.text: preferred by traders over every overland route
choices.rationale: Trader preferences for routes are not discussed.

explanation: The opening establishes elevation as the obstacle locks later removed.

stimulus.title: Stairs for Boats
stimulus.text: Rivers do not run level, and for centuries that simple fact blocked boats from traveling far inland. The lock changed things. A lock is a chamber with gates at each end; a boat enters, the gates close, and water is let in or drained out until the boat rises or falls to the next stretch of river. String several locks together, and a vessel can climb a hillside the way a person climbs a staircase. The engineering is humble, relying on nothing more exotic than gravity and patience, yet it knit distant towns into trading partners and turned shallow rivers into highways of commerce.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that customers valued Mr. Owusu's stall chiefly because they felt

choices.text: rushed through their purchases quickly
choices.rationale: Nothing suggests customers were rushed.

choices.text: uncertain about the quality of his produce
choices.rationale: His setting aside perfect produce implies quality, not doubt.

choices.text: personally recognized and cared for
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says they returned because, at his stall, 'they were known.'

choices.text: that his prices were the lowest available
choices.rationale: The passage explicitly says it was not his prices.

explanation: Customers valued feeling known and cared for.

stimulus.title: The Stall That Listened
stimulus.text: Every Saturday, Mr. Owusu set out the same vegetables on the same table, and for years his stall was just one among many. What set him apart, his daughter noticed, was not his prices but his memory. He recalled which customer's child disliked onions, who was cooking for a crowd that weekend, who had been ill and needed something gentle. He would set aside a perfect tomato for one regular and toss an extra handful of beans to another. People did not return only for the produce; they returned because, at his stall, they were known. When he finally retired, the market felt larger and lonelier, though not a single other stall had closed.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that merchants spread tall tales about spices in order to

choices.text: encourage as many new sailors as possible to enter the trade
choices.rationale: Tales discouraged rivals rather than recruiting newcomers.

choices.text: lower the prices that buyers were willing to pay
choices.rationale: High prices, not lower ones, served the merchants' interest.

choices.text: keep competitors away from their profitable trade routes
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says the tales were meant 'to discourage rivals.'

choices.text: teach customers the correct way to cook with spices
choices.rationale: The tales were about harvesting, not cooking instruction.

explanation: The tales served to protect routes by discouraging competitors.

stimulus.title: The Price of Pepper
stimulus.text: There was a time when a handful of black pepper could rival a handful of silver. The spice grew only in distant lands, and by the time it reached a European market it had passed through many hands, each adding a markup. Merchants guarded their routes jealously and spread tall tales about how spices were harvested, partly to discourage rivals. The high prices drove sailors to seek their own sea paths to the source, voyages that redrew the map of the world. In the end, the very abundance those voyages produced made spices ordinary, and the fortunes built on rarity quietly dissolved.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that, without lichens, a bare rock would

choices.text: produce richer soil than rock that lichens have colonized
choices.rationale: Lichen-free rock would have less, not richer, soil.

choices.text: remain forever incapable of supporting any plant life
choices.rationale: The passage does not say plant life would be forever impossible.

choices.text: take much longer to support mosses and small plants
choices.rationale: Correct. Since lichens form the first soil, their absence would slow later plant arrival.

choices.text: be colonized first by large trees instead of by mosses
choices.rationale: Large trees colonizing first contradicts the described order.

explanation: Because lichens create the first soil, their absence would delay later colonizers.

stimulus.title: First on the Rock
stimulus.text: When a bare rock is left exposed, the first life to arrive is often a lichen, a strange partnership of fungus and alga living as one. The fungus grips the stone and gathers moisture; the alga, sheltered inside, makes food from sunlight. Together they need no soil at all. As a lichen grows, it slowly releases acids that crack the rock surface, and its dead tissue mixes with grit to form the first thin crumbs of soil. Years later, mosses and small plants can take root in that beginning. The lichen will likely be crowded out by the very community it made possible, an unsung founder of the green world that follows.

prompt: The passage most strongly suggests that, before Gutenberg, identical copies of a text were

choices.text: rare, because copying by hand was slow and introduced small variations
choices.rationale: Correct. Hand-copying was slow and the passage stresses the novelty of identical printed copies.

choices.text: produced even faster by hand than printed copies later would be
choices.rationale: Hand-copying took a year, far slower than printing.

choices.text: common, since nearly every European town had its own busy copyists
choices.rationale: The passage implies the opposite of commonness.

choices.text: widely dismissed as worthless by the scholars of the period
choices.rationale: Scholars are said to prize handwritten books, not scorn them.

explanation: The contrast the passage draws implies hand-copied texts were neither fast nor uniform.

stimulus.title: Letters of Lead
stimulus.text: Before the 1450s, a book in Europe was copied by hand, a task that could occupy a scribe for a year. Johannes Gutenberg changed that arithmetic. By casting individual letters in metal, he could arrange them into a page, print hundreds of copies, then rearrange the same letters for the next page. The cost of a book did not fall overnight, and many scholars still prized handwritten volumes. But within fifty years, presses across the continent had produced millions of books. Ideas that once crept from city to city now traveled in bulk, and a reader in one town could hold the exact words read by a stranger far away.
